meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Someone's sitting in the shade today because someone planted a tree a long time ago'?
meta.ogDescription: A 1992 Buffett biography prints the exact line and credits a January 1991 statement. The proverb behind it is far older — 1868, and Cicero before that.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: b. 30 August 1930 · American investor; chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
answer.sourceLine: Buffett is credited with this exact sentence — word for word, contraction and all — in Andrew Kilpatrick’s 1992 biography Warren Buffett: The Good Guy of Wall Street, which prints it on page 288 and credits it to NewsInc., January 1991. That is a close, dated citation rather than a primary one: no transcript, letter or shareholder letter in Buffett’s own hand has been located for it, and the underlying thought was a common proverb in print long before he was born.

source.excerpt: Someone’s sitting in the shade today because someone planted a tree a long time ago. —NewsInc. January 1991.
trail: Antiquity — Cicero has Cato quote the poet Caecilius Statius: “Serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint”, he plants trees which will be of use to another age (de Senectute §24, Latin text ↗).
1868 — the Pall Mall Gazette prints a compact version labelled an “Indian proverb”: blessed is he who plants trees under whose shade he will never sit (Quote Investigator ↗).
1955 — Walter Lippmann, in Essays in The Public Philosophy, quotes the saying in passing as something already proverbial: old men plant trees they will never sit under (Quote Investigator ↗).
1991–1992 — Andrew Kilpatrick’s biography prints Buffett’s inverted version on page 288 and credits NewsInc., January 1991; Wikiquote cites the same January 1991 statement (Wikiquote ↗).
source.excerptNote: As reproduced by Quote Investigator from page 288 of the 1992 Kilpatrick biography, whose quotation chapter carries the credit line beneath the sentence. The circulating internet wording matches this printing exactly.

source.rightsHolder: Warren E. Buffett (the words); Andrew Kilpatrick and Donald I. Fine, Inc. (the 1992 biography in which they are documented)
source.rightsNote: This is a modern sentence from a living author: first documented in print in Kilpatrick’s 1992 biography and credited to a January 1991 statement, so it sits well inside US copyright — the 1931 public-domain cutoff is nowhere near it. The older proverb it reworks is free (Cicero’s Latin and the 1868 newspaper wording are long out of copyright), but Buffett’s particular phrasing is not; quote it with attribution rather than treating it as public domain.

author.name: Warren Buffett
author.heading: Who was doing the talking
author.metaLine: Born 1930 · American investor · chairman of Berkshire Hathaway
author.bio: Warren Edward Buffett was born in Omaha, Nebraska on 30 August 1930, learned value investing under Benjamin Graham at Graham-Newman, and founded Buffett Partnership Ltd. in 1956 before turning the failing textile maker Berkshire Hathaway into one of America’s largest conglomerates. He stepped down as Berkshire’s chief executive effective 1 January 2026, handing the job to Greg Abel while remaining chairman. His public voice is deliberately folksy — homely images, borrowed proverbs, plain arithmetic — which is exactly why sayings he repeated so often end up filed under his name as sayings he coined.

misattribution.heading: What Buffett did and didn’t invent
misattribution.intro: This is not a fake Buffett quote. The wording is his, and it is documented within about a year of his saying it. What gets misattributed is the idea: the internet routinely presents this as a Buffett original, and its close relatives get pinned on ancient Greeks who never said them.

items.who: Cicero, quoting the poet Caecilius Statius
items.why: Cato Maior de Senectute §24 reads “Serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint, ut ait Statius noster in Synephebis” — he plants trees which will be of use to another age (Latin text ↗).

Quote Investigator records the Pall Mall Gazette printing “Indian proverb, ‘Blessed is he who plants trees under whose shade he will never sit’” — in circulation decades before Buffett was born (Quote Investigator ↗).

items.who: “A society grows great when old men plant trees…” — called an ancient Greek proverb
items.why: Roger Pearse went looking for the Greek original and found none, concluding the real origin is most likely D. Elton Trueblood’s 1951 book The Life We Prize (Roger Pearse ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Buffett’s sentence is real and datable — a 1992 biography prints it verbatim and credits a January 1991 statement — but he was restating a proverb that was already in English newspapers in the 1860s and in Latin two millennia before that (Quote Investigator ↗).

context.heading: Why a fund manager was quoting a tree proverb
lead: Buffett’s whole public argument is that returns belong to people who wait. So a proverb about planting for a harvest you may never sit under is not decoration in his mouth — it is the thesis, compressed to one sentence a reader remembers after the annual report is closed.

What makes the line travel is the pronoun. Older versions of the proverb are addressed to the planter (“blessed is he who plants trees under whose shade he will never sit”). Buffett flipped the point of view to the person in the shade — the beneficiary, not the benefactor — which turns a lesson about generosity into a lesson about inheritance and compounding.
context.detailsSummary: How old is the underlying proverb?
detailsBody: Older than English. Cicero, in Cato Maior de Senectute §24, quotes the Roman poet Caecilius Statius: “serit arbores, quae alteri saeclo prosint” — he plants trees which will be of use to another age.

Quote Investigator’s survey of the saying runs through Thomas Fuller’s Gnomologia (1732), nineteenth-century newspapers, an 1866 sermon by the French theologian Hyacinthe Loyson, an 1868 Pall Mall Gazette item that labelled a compact version an “Indian proverb,” and mid-century instances from Elton Trueblood (1951) and Walter Lippmann (1955), before reaching Buffett in 1992.
context.pull: The old proverb praises the planter. Buffett’s version addresses the person already sitting in the shade.
